description: A DEBUGGING fixture, not a grading dataset. Two compact briefs that stay cheap but leave the judge room to differentiate: each demands working interactions (a filter, buttons that change state, a dynamic detail route) and concrete data realism, so a weak prototype scores visibly below a strong one instead of everything saturating the top anchor band. Both exercise the code track's nav and interaction checks. Scores from this dataset are NOT comparable to ten-industries and must never be used to calibrate a baseline or judge a prompt change. Row ids are stable across every stage.

rows.prompt: Build a small internal appointment viewer for a two-provider family clinic. Exactly 4 pages: Schedule, Patient Detail, Providers, Settings. Keep it compact — at most 5 example rows per table and short prose — but make it WORK: the Schedule page needs a text search box that filters the appointment table as you type, and a status filter (All / Confirmed / Checked-in / No-show) as clickable buttons; each appointment row links to Patient Detail via a dynamic route like #/patient/:id, and the detail page must render the clicked patient's data, not one hardcoded record. Use realistic clinic data — plausible patient names, appointment times on a real-looking day, provider names, statuses — never lorem ipsum or 'Patient A'. No template or design system has been selected; use your own judgment, plain and functional.

Build a small internal expense-approval console for a finance team. Exactly 4 pages: Inbox, Expense Detail, Reports, Settings. Keep it compact — at most 5 example rows per table and short prose — but make it WORK: the Inbox needs filter buttons (All / Pending / Approved / Rejected) that actually filter the table; Expense Detail is reached via a dynamic route like #/expense/:id and shows the clicked expense with Approve and Reject buttons that visibly update its status badge on the page; Reports shows a simple total-by-category breakdown consistent with the Inbox data. Use realistic finance data — merchant names, plausible amounts with currency, submission dates, employee names — never round placeholder numbers. No template or design system has been selected; use your own judgment, plain and functional.

Build a slotting-optimisation workbench for Granite Peak Distribution's pick floor. Pages: Slot Grid, SKU Detail via #/sku/:id, Replenishment, Velocity Report, Moves, Settings. Slot Grid lists 20 pick slots (aisle-bay-level code, SKU, on-hand, daily picks, fill %) filterable by aisle and by a 'below reorder point' toggle, with SKU text search. SKU Detail shows the clicked SKU's velocity history table, current slot, and a 'Queue move' action selecting a suggested better slot — queued moves appear on the Moves page and flag the source row on the Slot Grid. Velocity Report's top-10 must be derivable from the grid data. Realistic SKUs, case quantities, aisle codes like A-07-2.

Build a dispatch board for Meridian Field Services' HVAC technician network. Pages: Dispatch Board, Job Detail via #/job/:id, Technicians, Parts, SLA Report, Settings. Dispatch Board lists 18 open jobs (job code, customer, site, priority, technician, promised-by, status) filterable by priority and by an 'unassigned only' toggle, with customer text search. Job Detail shows the clicked job's timeline, required parts with on-hand counts, and an 'Assign technician' action choosing from technicians whose skills match the job — assigning must set the technician on the Dispatch Board, drop the job out of the 'unassigned only' filter, and add it to that technician's load on the Technicians page. The SLA Report's at-risk count must be derivable from the board's promised-by times. Settings holds dispatch defaults: a promise-window select, an SLA at-risk threshold input that the SLA Report reads, and a toggle for skill-matched assignment only. Realistic job codes like MFS-4417, site addresses, and part numbers.
